paragraphs.mainIdea: Anna's mother died the morning after Caleb was born.
paragraphs.simple: The story Caleb knows is finished, but Anna did not tell him what she really thought: that Caleb was plain and smelled bad, and that their mother died the next morning. That last part was the worst thing.

paragraphs.mainIdea: Sarah writes that she loves the sea, works hard, and is not gentle or quiet in manner.
paragraphs.simple: Sarah writes that she has always loved living by the sea, but now she feels she must move. She says the sea is as far east as she can go, and her choice is small. She is strong and works hard and will travel. She warns Papa that she is not mild mannered.

paragraphs.simple: Sarah writes about the colors of the sea: blue and gray and green. Her brother William is a fisherman. When he is in the middle of a fog-bound sea, the water has a color with no name. She is sending Anna a book of sea birds.

paragraphs.mainIdea: Sarah offers to teach Caleb to swim in the cow pond.
paragraphs.simple: Sarah is surprised that Caleb cannot swim. She says she will teach him in the cow pond.

paragraphs.context: It gleams like the sun on glass. There are waves.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sarah describes the sea to Caleb: salty, wide, gleaming, with waves.
paragraphs.simple: Sarah tells Caleb what the sea is like. It is salt. It stretches out as far as you can see. It gleams like the sun on glass. There are waves.

paragraphs.context: The fields had turned to a sea that gleamed like sun
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anna dreams the fields have become a sea, and Sarah is happy.
paragraphs.simple: They climb the bank, dry themselves, and lie in the grass again. Anna falls asleep and dreams a perfect dream: the fields have turned into a sea that gleams like sun on glass. And Sarah is happy.

paragraphs.context: The house is hers now. Not mine any longer.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sarah admits she misses her brother, her home, and her aunts.
paragraphs.simple: Sarah says she misses her brother William. But he is married, and the house is hers now, not Sarah's any longer. She also misses her three old aunts, who all squawk together like crows at dawn.

paragraphs.context: “Try,” said Maggie. “You must have a garden.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Maggie urges Sarah to plant a garden wherever she is.
paragraphs.simple: Maggie says, “Try. You must have a garden.”

paragraphs.context: bringing Sarah the first roses of summer
paragraphs.mainIdea: Papa brings Sarah the summer's first roses.
paragraphs.simple: Just before the rain, Papa comes, bringing Sarah the first roses of summer.

paragraphs.context: strange clouds hung in the northwest, low and black and green
paragraphs.mainIdea: After the rain, strange green-black clouds gather and the air goes still.
paragraphs.simple: The rain comes and passes. But strange clouds hang in the northwest, low and black and green. And the air grows still.

paragraphs.context: “Why does she want to go to town by herself?”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Caleb worries that Sarah wants to go to town alone so she can leave them.
paragraphs.simple: Caleb asks Anna why Sarah wants to go to town by herself. He wonders: is it to leave them?

paragraphs.context: Sarah and Papa stood in the barn doorway, wet to the skin.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sarah and Papa return to the barn soaked, carrying the chickens and an armful of roses.
paragraphs.simple: Sarah has run from the barn into a sheet of rain, and Papa has followed her. The sheep mill around the barn, bleating. Then, as the thunder pounds and lightning cracks close by, Sarah and Papa stand in the barn doorway, wet to the skin. Papa carries Sarah's chickens, and Sarah carries an armful of summer roses.

paragraphs.context: “We have squalls in Maine, too,” she said. “Just like
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sarah comforts Papa, saying storms like this happen in Maine too.
paragraphs.simple: Sarah says they have squalls in Maine too, just like this. She tells Jacob it will be all right.

paragraphs.context: It was white and gleaming for as far as we looked, like
paragraphs.mainIdea: After the storm, the hail-covered ground looks white and gleaming like the sea.
paragraphs.simple: They sleep in the hay all night, waking when the wind is wild and sleeping again when it is quiet. At dawn there is the sudden sound of hail, like stones tossed against the barn. They watch the ice marbles bounce on the ground. When it is over they open the barn door and walk out into the early-morning light. The hail crunches and melts beneath their feet. It is white and gleaming for as far as they look, like sun on glass. Like the sea.

paragraphs.context: the wild roses were scattered on the ground
paragraphs.mainIdea: After the storm, everything is quiet. The wild roses lie on the ground as if a wedding had been held there, and Sarah is glad she picked some before the storm.
paragraphs.simple: After the storm, it was very quiet. The dogs ate small pieces of ice (hailstones) off the ground. Seal, the cat, walked around the dogs and jumped up on the fence to clean her fur. A tree had fallen near the cow pond. Wild roses were lying all over the ground, as if a wedding had come and ended there. Sarah only said, "I am glad I saved an armful," meaning she was glad she had picked many roses before the storm.

paragraphs.context: I remembered another time when a wagon had taken Mama away
paragraphs.mainIdea: Watching Sarah drive off reminds Anna of the day a wagon took her own mother away. Her mother never came home again.
paragraphs.simple: Caleb and Anna watched Sarah leave from the porch. Caleb held Anna's hand, and the dogs lay down next to them. It was sunny. The scene made Anna remember another sunny day long ago, when a wagon had taken Mama away. Mama had never come back.

paragraphs.context: when the preacher asks if he will have Sarah for his wife
paragraphs.mainIdea: The family has a warm evening meal by candlelight. Soon Papa will marry Sarah, and his answer at the wedding will be "Ayuh," which means "yes."
paragraphs.simple: The four of them, Papa, Sarah, Caleb, and Anna, eat their night meal by candlelight. Sarah bought candles, flower seeds for her garden, and a book of songs in town. It is late; Caleb is almost asleep by his plate, and Sarah is smiling at Papa. Soon there will be a wedding. Papa says that when the preacher asks if he will have Sarah for his wife, he will answer, "Ayuh," which is a way of saying "yes."

paragraphs.context: Papa will stretch a rope from the door to the barn
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anna pictures their future together: a hard, cold winter when Papa will tie a rope from the door to the barn so no one gets lost, and Sarah's sea picture hanging on the wall. Sarah will stay with them.
paragraphs.simple: Anna thinks about what will come: autumn, then a cold winter with strong winds like the sea wind in Maine, where Sarah used to live. They will look for nests of curls and keep dried flowers all winter. When big storms come, Papa will tie a rope from the house door to the barn, so they can hold it and find their way and not get lost when they feed the sheep, the cows, Jack, and Old Bess. Sarah's chickens may even live inside the house. Sarah's drawing of the sea, blue and gray and green, will hang on the wall. There will be songs, old ones and new. Seal, the cat with yellow eyes, will be there. And Sarah, plain and tall, will be there.

paragraphs.context: The water dried up, the fields so dry that the leaves fell like dust
paragraphs.mainIdea: Joshua remembers a terrible drought long ago: no water, fields so dry that leaves fell like dust, and strong winds. His grandfather packed up the whole family and left.
paragraphs.simple: Joshua speaks in a low, quiet voice. He looks out over the land with eyes that seem far away, as if his mind is somewhere else. He says Maine is probably green. They really need rain here. He remembers a long time ago: the water dried up, the fields were so dry that the leaves fell like dust, and then strong winds came. His grandfather packed up everything and left with his family, and never came back.

paragraphs.context: Our names are written in this land
paragraphs.mainIdea: Papa says they will never leave: they were born here, and they belong to this land so deeply it is as if their names are written in it.
paragraphs.simple: Papa says to Sarah, "We would never leave. We were born here. Our names are written in this land." He means they belong to this place completely; their family history is part of the land itself, as if their names were written in the earth.

paragraphs.context: Justin had gone to Europe to fight in the war
paragraphs.mainIdea: Everyone is quiet because Justin, Anna's boyfriend, has gone to fight in a war, and no one jokes about him anymore. Anna works with Doctor Sam, Justin's father, because it makes her feel closer to Justin.
paragraphs.simple: Everyone became quiet. The narrator used to make fun of Anna about her boyfriend, Justin, calling him "Just-In-Time." But he does not do that anymore. Justin had gone to Europe to fight in the war, so now no one teases Anna. The narrator thinks Anna worked for Doctor Sam because Justin was Doctor Sam's son. Working with Sam made Anna feel closer to Justin.

paragraphs.context: So many have died. And you see the worst of it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sarah is afraid for Anna: many people are sick and many have died, and Anna, who works with the doctor, sees the sickest people and the worst of it.
paragraphs.simple: Sarah puts her arm around Anna and says, "So many people are sick. So many have died. And you see the worst of it." Anna works with Doctor Sam, so she sees the sickest people and the saddest things. Sarah is worried about her.

paragraphs.context: In the quiet, the prairie seemed larger than ever
paragraphs.mainIdea: The narrator stands watching Papa's wagon roll away in the falling snow. In the quiet, the big open prairie feels larger than ever.
paragraphs.simple: The narrator stands watching the wheels of Papa's wagon leave small tracks on the wet road. All around him is the soft, surprising sound of snow falling. In the quiet, the prairie, the great open grassland, seems larger than ever.

paragraphs.context: Caleb has always called Mama Sarah. My mama is not Caleb’s
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cassie explains that Sarah is her real mother, but not Caleb's. Caleb and Anna met Sarah before she married Papa, so they still call her Sarah. Cassie calls her Mama.
paragraphs.simple: Caleb has always called Mama "Sarah." Sarah is Cassie's real mother, but she is not Caleb's real mother. When Sarah first came to meet Papa, before they were married, Caleb and Anna called her Sarah, and they still do. Cassie calls her Mama. Maybe one day Cassie will call her Sarah too.

paragraphs.context: Mama once said he looked like an angel
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack has pretty, curly, light-colored hair, and Mama once said he looked like an angel. But Grandfather says Jack usually does not behave like one.
paragraphs.simple: Jack runs out of the barn, with Papa and their dog Lottie behind him. His pale, light-colored hair is long and curly around his face. Mama once said he looked like an angel, a beautiful, good child. But Grandfather said that most of the time, Jack did not act like one; he was not always good and gentle.

paragraphs.context: He never showed Grandfather his temper
paragraphs.mainIdea: Surprisingly, Jack is gentle and sweet with Grandfather: he never shows anger there, loves his stories and songs, and Grandfather is Jack's favorite person.
paragraphs.simple: The surprising thing was that with Grandfather, Jack did act like an angel. He never frowned at Grandfather. He never showed his bad temper to Grandfather. Every evening he sat on Grandfather's lap and made Grandfather tell him a story and sing to him. From the very beginning, Grandfather had been Jack's favorite person.

sentences.context: Not because he meant to, but because he had been thinking of it
sentences.simple: He said it in a harsh way. He did not mean to sound harsh. He had been thinking about it for a long time.
sentences.grammar: Two short sentences stand in for a full one: the repeated words 'he said it harshly' are left out, and only the reasons are given, joined by 'not ... but ...'.

sentences.context: For the twentieth time this month. The hundredth time this year?
sentences.simple: I was telling him again. I had already told him for the twentieth time this month, maybe the hundredth time this year, and I had been telling him for the past few years.
sentences.grammar: Three verb-less fragments with no verb of their own; they borrow 'I told him' from the sentence before and only count how many times.

sentences.context: their footprints are much larger than hers
sentences.simple: Dogs' footprints are much bigger than a cat's footprints.
sentences.grammar: A shortened comparison: 'hers' stands in for 'her footprints,' and the repeated words 'are' are left out after 'than.'

sentences.context: Tell them I sing was all it said.
sentences.simple: The note at the bottom of the letter said only this: 'Tell them I sing.'
sentences.grammar: A whole quoted sentence, 'Tell them I sing,' is used as the subject of 'was all it said' -- it is the note's only message.

sentences.context: My father did not see her look, but I did.
sentences.simple: My father did not notice how Sarah looked. But I noticed.
sentences.grammar: In 'but I did,' the repeated verb phrase is left out: 'did' stands for 'did see her look.'

sentences.context: the windbreak of Russian olive that Mama had planted long ago
sentences.simple: The wagon went around the windmill, the barn, and the row of Russian olive trees. Mama had planted those trees long ago.
sentences.grammar: 'that Mama had planted long ago' is a defining clause with no comma: it tells which trees are meant, not just extra information.

sentences.context: He brushed his hair so slick and shiny that Caleb laughed
sentences.simple: He brushed his hair until it was so smooth and shiny that Caleb laughed.
sentences.grammar: 'so' + describing words + 'that' clause: the 'that' part gives the result of how slick and shiny his hair was.

sentences.context: Papa was quiet and shy with Sarah, and so was I.
sentences.simple: Papa was quiet and shy around Sarah. I was quiet and shy, too.
sentences.grammar: After 'so,' the sentence flips: instead of 'and I was so,' the verb 'was' comes before the subject 'I.'

sentences.context: even Papa, who sang as if he had never stopped singing
sentences.simple: She taught the song to everyone, even Papa. Papa sang as though he had never stopped singing in all the years before.
sentences.grammar: 'as if' + past perfect ('had never stopped') paints a picture that is not literally true: he had stopped, but he sang like someone who never had.

sentences.context: Next to the barn was Papa’s mound of hay for bedding
sentences.simple: Papa's big pile of hay for bedding was next to the barn.
sentences.grammar: The place phrase 'Next to the barn' comes first, so the subject ('Papa's mound of hay') moves after the verb 'was' -- the sentence is flipped.

sentences.context: is almost as fine as sliding down the sand dunes into the sea
sentences.simple: Sliding down our hay pile is almost as good as sliding down real sand dunes into the sea.
sentences.grammar: 'as fine as' sets the two kinds of sliding side by side as equals; 'almost' softens it to 'nearly as good.'

sentences.context: jump over rocks and gullies, the sheep behind him, stiff legged and fast
sentences.simple: Caleb jumped over rocks and ditches. The sheep ran behind him, their legs stiff, moving fast.
sentences.grammar: 'the sheep behind him, stiff legged and fast' is a verb-less tag-on: a noun ('the sheep') plus describing phrases, with no verb of its own.

sentences.context: There is always something to miss, no matter where you are
sentences.simple: Wherever you live, there will always be something you miss.
sentences.grammar: 'no matter where' opens a concession clause: the first part stays true in every place.

sentences.context: as the thunder pounded and the wind rose and there was the terrible crackling
sentences.simple: Then Sarah and Papa stood in the barn doorway, completely wet. At the same time, thunder pounded, wind rose, and lightning crackled terribly nearby.
sentences.grammar: Three short clauses are stacked inside one 'as' time-clause before the main action finally arrives.

sentences.context: We slept in the hay all night, waking when the wind was wild
sentences.simple: We slept in the hay all night. We woke up when the wind was wild, and slept again when it grew quiet.
sentences.grammar: 'waking ...' and 'sleeping again ...' are -ing phrases with no subject of their own; they borrow 'we' and describe what 'we' kept doing.

sentences.context: when the preacher asks if he will have Sarah for his wife
sentences.simple: When the preacher asks Papa whether he will take Sarah as his wife, Papa will answer, 'Ayuh.'
sentences.grammar: Reported speech inside a time clause: 'asks if ...' reports the preacher's future question, and 'he will answer' sits inside the 'when' clause.

sentences.context: I hardly know what they look like anymore
sentences.simple: I almost do not know what they look like now.
sentences.grammar: 'hardly' already makes the sentence negative ('almost not'), so 'anymore' adds the time change without another 'not.'

sentences.context: That she does,” said Joshua, smiling.
sentences.simple: Joshua smiled and agreed strongly: 'Yes, she certainly does live here.'
sentences.grammar: 'That she does' echoes Caleb's words with 'that' pushed to the front and 'does' standing in for the repeated verb 'lives here.'

sentences.context: the fields so dry that the leaves fell like dust
sentences.simple: The fields were so dry that the leaves fell like dust.
sentences.grammar: The verb 'were' is left out after 'the fields' -- 'the fields (were) so dry that ...' -- inside a chain of short picture-clauses.

sentences.context: I used to tease Anna about her boyfriend, Justin
sentences.simple: In the past I often teased Anna about her boyfriend, Justin, but I do not do it now.
sentences.grammar: 'used to' + verb marks a past habit that has stopped; it does not mean 'I am used to.'

sentences.context: Everyone’s not a writer, Caleb,” said Anna.
sentences.simple: Anna said, 'Caleb, not everyone is a writer. But everyone can write.'
sentences.grammar: 'Everyone's not a writer' puts the 'not' after 'everyone is,' but it means 'not everyone is a writer' -- the negative covers only some people, not all.

sentences.context: a time when Cassie would answer me and give away her hiding place
sentences.simple: Once, Cassie always called back to me, and her answer showed me where she was hiding.
sentences.grammar: 'would answer' is not future here: 'would' + verb marks something she regularly did in the past.

sentences.context: Martha, Eleni, Princess, Mary Louise, Pudgie, and Boots, can float into the barn
sentences.simple: Her notebook said Grandfather and Caleb dug deep rivers in the mud, so the cows could float into the barn to eat. Then she listed all the cows' names.
sentences.grammar: The long list of names is only a renaming tag for 'the cows' -- it adds no new action, only tells which cows.

sentences.context: I couldn’t pay attention. Neither could Ian or Min or Grace.
sentences.simple: I could not pay attention. Ian, Min, and Grace could not pay attention either.
sentences.grammar: 'Neither could ...' flips the order after a negative: the verb 'could' comes before the subject, and it means 'also not.'

sentences.context: The surprise was that Jack did act like an angel around Grandfather
sentences.simple: What surprised her was this: around Grandfather, Jack really did behave like an angel.
sentences.grammar: 'The surprise was that ...' puts the news first, and 'did act' uses extra 'did' for emphasis -- he truly behaved well.
